voice_definition.pov_approach: Multi-POV close third-person limited, past tense. Primary POV: Ben Skywalker (~28 of 38 chapters). Selected secondary POV: Talon Veyr (Ch 8 'Waste Runoff', Ch 22 'Maro Tess'). Single-chapter dedicated POVs: Commander Elya Rane (Ch 1 hook, through her death), Sela Dray (Ch 25 'Some Places Remember Too Loudly', Ch 28 'Tavi'), Aevyn Soris (Ch 30 'Opening'), Colonel Maro Tess (opens Ch 20 PP2 'Containment'; full POV Ch 37 'A Board Cleared'). Split-POV chapters with alternating in-chapter Ben/Talon close-third: Ch 7 'Break Cover', Ch 9 'Storm Line' (FPP), Ch 14-15 archive sequence (PP1), Ch 16 'No Good Version' (Midpoint), Ch 33 'The Flood'. Ch 38 'White-Blue Spark' is a distant/image POV — no character interior — the final spark below the broken Glasswell. POV labels stable per chapter per Chapter Outlines v4.0; refinement deferred to first-draft pass.
voice_definition.prose_register: Commercial post-war conspiracy thriller in space-opera register. Cinematic clarity, adventure momentum, lived-in technology, dry humor, mythic Force awe when earned. Reader pleasure before theme — the book reads first as a tense Star Wars adventure (murder, prison break, uneasy partnership, archive attack, respected charity with a hidden inner ring, offworld Force-site climax, morally dangerous ending) and only secondarily as a meditation on Jacen/Caedus, trauma, restraint, and dangerous knowledge. Sentence-level prose sits in the Allston/Zahn commercial neighborhood — clean, propulsive, short paragraphs, intelligent characters who sound intelligent without lecturing. Technical / institutional detail handled as character not lecture in the Traviss neighborhood. Aevyn's interior precision-with-buried-wound anchors to Tana French's controlled-mystery interiority as a non-SW touchstone. NO specific Star Wars author is imitated. CHARACTER-FIRST RULE (bible §0C): no line wiser, cooler, or more poetic than the character would naturally be.

reference_authors.author: Aaron Allston
reference_authors.what_to_emulate: REGISTER SAMPLE — NOT a voice template. Use as sentence-level rhythm and dialogue-density reference for Talon Veyr's voice and the Ben/Talon partnership tempo. Emulate: dialogue-forward scene construction; ensemble POV piloting; dry, integrated humor that moves the scene rather than decorates it; political/institutional worldbuilding delivered through argument rather than exposition; prison-and-procedural texture that earns its tension through small physical details (sea wall, storm shutters, camera lag, guard habits); buddy-cop friction that doesn't dilute serious stakes. Benchmark works: Wraith Squadron, Iron Fist, Mercy Kill; Betrayal (LotF book 1) for ensemble POV piloting circa this era.
reference_authors.what_to_avoid: Do NOT lean into the comic-relief register when scenes are darkening — the book's Act 3 is genuinely grim and the Talon humor valve must shut. Do NOT copy Allston's chapter-as-vignette structural rhythm; The Unfinished Shadow runs chapters as dramatic units of variable scene count, not Allston-style rotating-cast snapshots. Do NOT imitate his prose as a voice template; the bible forbids author-imitation and Talon must remain a specific character, not 'an Allston wraith'.

reference_authors.author: Timothy Zahn
reference_authors.what_to_emulate: REGISTER SAMPLE — NOT a voice template. Use as sentence-level rhythm and prose-discipline reference for Colonel Maro Tess's calm operational antagonist register and for Ben Skywalker's POV interiority discipline. Emulate: clean, precise, efficient prose; dialogue that advances plot and reveals character simultaneously; intelligent antagonists who sound intelligent without lecturing; tactical clarity in action scenes; short paragraphs; sentences that do their work and get out of the way. Benchmark works: Heir to the Empire, Specter of the Past as register anchors. Working rule from the Ruusan voice block: 'When in doubt about prose choices, ask whether this sentence would appear in a Zahn novel — if it is ornate or introspective beyond a line or two, the answer is no.'
reference_authors.what_to_avoid: Zahn's prose can run emotionally cool — functional rather than felt. Ben's POV needs warmth that Zahn-clear sentences alone do not carry; carry the warmth through behavior, body language, and the small private moments (Ben covering an old GAG sender code before he realizes; Ben taking the half-sandwich from a Civitas coworker; Ben tightening his hand around the table edge when he answers Luke 'Somewhere it can't hurt anyone'). Do NOT import Specter-era political-thriller framing — this is a conspiracy thriller, not a senate-procedural.

reference_authors.author: Karen Traviss
reference_authors.what_to_emulate: REGISTER SAMPLE — NOT a voice template. Use as sentence-level rhythm and texture reference for the GAG investigation register: institutional and procedural detail handled as CHARACTER rather than as lecture. Emulate: how a former operator narrates logistics, manifests, transfer corrections, and quarantine classifications in the same breath as fear and exhaustion; compressed expert dialogue between Iressa and Talon that communicates competence through implication; respect for non-Force-sensitive characters' moral weight (Talon, Iressa, Elya, Sela). Benchmark works: Republic Commando series (Hard Contact through Order 66); Imperial Commando: 501st; her Mandalorian texture as a model for institution-as-character.
reference_authors.what_to_avoid: Do NOT import Traviss's polemical authorial framing — the drafter must not editorialize about the Jedi Order through the narrator. The investigation IS critical of GAG and the Vigil (by design) but the critique lands through PERSONAL CONSEQUENCE (Elya's dead body, Iressa's lost respectable life, Talon's ruined record) rather than thesis. Do NOT lean on Mandalorian iconography or Mando'a vocabulary — there are no Mandalorians on-page in Book 1.

reference_authors.author: Tana French
reference_authors.what_to_emulate: NON-STAR-WARS REGISTER SAMPLE. Use exclusively as a sentence-level rhythm reference for Aevyn Soris's precision-with-buried-wound interior register and for Ben's post-PP2 emotional pressure passages. Emulate: controlled, exact interiority that lets the wound surface in fragments rather than confession; long sentences that trail into pause-marked fragments when the speaker brushes the thing they will not say; mystery-genre discipline of revealing only what the POV character can bear to know in this moment. Benchmark works: In the Woods, The Likeness, Broken Harbor.
reference_authors.what_to_avoid: Do NOT import French's contemporary urban-Ireland setting register or her police-procedural beats — Aevyn is not a detective and the Force is not a forensic system. Do NOT import French's deliberate withholding of the central explanation (e.g., the Woods conclusion) — Book 1 must resolve its central case cleanly; only the morally dangerous threads stay open. Use French ONLY for sentence-level rhythm in Aevyn's Ch 30 POV and the corridor-flashback fragment, never as a structural model.

character_voices.Ben Skywalker: REGISTER: controlled, direct, young under pressure, defensive when seen too clearly. Polite but rusty around ordinary civilian small talk — can handle danger better than a lunchroom conversation. Best emotional lines are SHORT. RHYTHM TARGET: controlled-direct. Short emotional lines (2-6 words). Mid-length action sentences. Interior reflection lands in two-to-three-sentence bursts before behavior takes over. Long introspective passages are an anti-pattern — show, then move. AVOIDANCE HABITS: says 'I'm fine' too quickly; moves into action before emotional conversation can catch him; covers old wounds with competence; gets defensive when Luke is right too gently; notices exits and threat angles without meaning to. GOOD: "I said I've got it." / "That doesn't make it better." / "I know what it looks like." / "I was fourteen." "That's not an excuse. It's a fact." / "I'm not doing that to her." / "Gone where?" "Somewhere it can't hurt anyone." "That wasn't what I asked." "I know." AVOID: "I fear that Jacen's shadow still lives within me." Never have Ben repeatedly ask himself 'Am I becoming Jacen?' — let other characters react to him before he admits what they saw. BETTER: Ben looked at the hostage, then at Vara, and hated that he knew another way. VULNERABLE TO: mentions of Mara; Jacen's old training phrases; Luke seeing through him; Talon refusing to let him simplify GAG; Aevyn knowing private Jacen-shaped details. CHARACTER DANGER: wants meaning, not darkness — his most dangerous choices are also his most defensible ones.
character_voices.Talon Veyr: REGISTER: quick, irreverent, practical, never solemn unless the valve shuts. When he does say something serious it lands because he avoids doing that. Jokes are not random — they MUST move the scene, hide fear, or puncture solemnity. RHYTHM TARGET: fast-irreverent. Comma-heavy. Sentence fragments allowed for tempo. Dialogue-forward; interior in short bursts. Long sentences arrive ONLY when the valve shuts and the joke fails. AVOIDANCE HABITS: jokes before answering honestly; deflects gratitude; makes fear sound like irritation; turns vulnerability into a complaint; calls Ben 'Skywalker' when guarded, 'Ben' when trust slips through. STOPS JOKING when: Tess, prison routines, civilian deaths tied to his old authorizations, children inside security systems, Ben being fourteen in GAG, anyone saying 'necessary' too smoothly. GOOD: "Good. I love careful. Careful is what people say before asking me to crawl through something illegal." / "That's not a lockdown. That's a kidnapping with paperwork." / "'I'm fine.' 'You're bleeding.' 'I'm expanding the definition.'" / "Any room with that many clean badges has done something expensive to deserve them." / "I was in government work. We called that plausible." / "He said logistics would teach me scale. It mostly taught me how easy it is to lose people in paperwork." AVOID: "My trauma has left me distrustful of institutions." BETTER: "No one builds that many exits unless they plan to leave someone else behind." CRAFT NOTE: let the jokes occasionally fail — when Talon stays silent the pressure underneath should land.
character_voices.Iressa Vossk: REGISTER: brisk, transactional, office-cynical. Uses invoices, fees, corporate language, and professional irritation as armor. Sounds like someone with a calendar invite and a hidden blaster she will deny owning. RHYTHM TARGET: clipped-bureaucratic. Sentence-level efficiency. Short declaratives interspersed with professional irritation. Long sentences only when reconstructing manifests — and even those compress technical detail into character beat. AVOIDANCE HABITS: denies knowing people she clearly knows; charges fees when frightened; uses professional language to describe criminal skills; pretends not to care while preserving names and evidence; keeps exits she insists do not exist. GOOD: "I have a calendar invite in twelve minutes and a fake name with dental benefits. Start by apologizing." / "'I do compliance.' 'You forge records.' 'That is an ugly word for user-corrected metadata.'" / "This was not a clerical duplicate. Someone cloned a shipment identity and dressed a secret up as medical cargo." / "Jedi complication fee." / "'Talon owes me money.' 'How much?' 'That depends on how irritating he is in the next five minutes.'" AVOID: "I built a fragile life to hide from my past." BETTER: "Do you know how hard it is to get a respectable job after a war crime adjacency problem?" DEATH RULE: she dies actively denying the enemy a clean copy and transmitting the dying package. NOT a martyrdom lesson for Ben. Her final beat is herself — practical irritation, file anger, or one last debt/fee joke rather than sentimental sacrifice.
character_voices.Aelia Vandros: REGISTER: warm, precise, composed, socially powerful. Rarely raises her voice — her danger is credibility, not volume. Never publicly defends 'Darth Caedus'; civic / memorial / therapeutic language only (clarity, resilience, steadiness, continuity, preparation). Privately thinks of Jacen as Jacen. RHYTHM TARGET: warm-civic-controlled. Longer sentences than the other antagonists. Subordinate clauses for graciousness. Never two emphatic words in a row. Polished cadence that beats Ben socially before he understands he is losing. AVOIDANCE HABITS: translates moral horror into civic language; corrects simplifications gently; uses grief as both truth and shield; remembers names; writes condolence notes by hand; uses courtesy as control. GOOD: "I write to the families every year, Master Skywalker. Not because it heals them. It does not. But because someone should remember the names without needing a trial transcript." / "You are very young. That is not an insult. It is only a fact people forget when reading your family name." / "I am not asking you to forgive him. I am asking whether the dead are better served by pretending no one learned anything at all." / "The crimes were real. So were the failures that came before them." AVOID: "Jacen's crimes contained necessary truths." BETTER: "Some people hesitate until the casualty lists become easier to print than the orders." CRAFT NOTE: Aelia must beat Ben SOCIALLY before she is exposed operationally. If she becomes obviously evil too early she loses power. Warmth must remain real through the end.
character_voices.Bren Korda: REGISTER: clean, controlled, administrative menace. Smooth with superiors, polite in public, cruel through process, never openly messy when witnesses matter. More frightening when he makes cruelty sound appropriate; never a thug. RHYTHM TARGET: procedural-clean. Declarative sentences in complete-paragraph units. Bureaucratic rhythm: the form of concern with the function of refusal. AVOIDANCE HABITS: hides threats inside procedure; uses proper channels as weapons; makes others seem unreasonable for noticing danger; treats compassion as a security vulnerability. GOOD: "You are welcome to file a complaint. I can recommend the appropriate office." / "This is a memorial facility, Master Skywalker. I would ask you to remember where you are." / "Security is mostly preventing emotional people from making permanent decisions." / "Veyr. I assumed they had better locks." AVOID: "I am corrupt but respectable." BETTER: "Procedure exists to protect everyone. Even people who find it inconvenient." CRAFT NOTE: Talon's humor THINS or stops in any room Korda enters — Korda makes Talon feel seen in the worst way.
character_voices.Colonel Maro Tess: REGISTER: plain, calm, operational. NO villain poetry. Does not posture. Does not explain more than required. Uses Talon's first name when it asserts ownership — Talon hates it. RHYTHM TARGET: plain-operational. Declarative. No subordinate clauses for ornament. Each sentence carries one fact or one instruction. Maximum economy. Two-word lines are allowed and preferred when they land. AVOIDANCE HABITS: turns people into categories (exposed, recoverable, lost); treats failures as logistics; removes sentiment from decisions; uses first names when asserting ownership. GOOD: "'Korda can carry the public version.' 'He's dead.' 'That helps.'" / "'Iresh failed.' 'Completely?' 'No.'" / "Skywalker moved as trained." / "Do not punish panic. Use it or remove it." / "Talon always did understand exits." / "You saved the people in front of you. You lost the people I needed you to think about." AVOID: "History belongs to those who manage its losses." BETTER: "The report needs one responsible name. Korda's will do." CRAFT NOTE: Tess is terrifying because he is NORMAL. Failure does not embarrass him; it gives him new categories.
character_voices.Aevyn Soris: REGISTER: quiet, exact, wounded underneath. Speaks SOFTER when angry, not louder. Dislikes generic praise. Replays exact wording of old dismissals. Aligns tools at exact angles. Refuses 'Caedus' — uses 'Jacen' only. RHYTHM TARGET: quiet-precise. Sentences trimmed to load-bearing words. Periods over commas. Long sentences land ONLY when the wound flashes through — then trail off into pause-marked fragment. Tana French interiority register; the corridor flashback surfaces as image, never speech. AVOIDANCE HABITS: aligns tools at exact angles; corrects language when others are imprecise; controls his tone carefully; refuses broad emotional confession; treats his unstable lightsaber like an argument he keeps trying to perfect; replays the exact wording of old dismissals when alone. WHAT MAKES HIM CRACK: being called weak or insufficient; generic praise (he knows how to recognize the polite no underneath); Jacen reduced to only Caedus; Ben having Jedi training, family, Jacen's primary attention, and survival; Ben using Jacen's lessons while denying Aevyn the holocron; any reference to 'placement' or 'measuring'. GOOD: "They said I had patience. They meant no." / "Do not call him that." / "He taught you to count exits before faces, didn't he?" / "You buried the lesson. You still used it." / "The Jedi measure what they can use. Jacen measured what could grow." AVOID: "The Jedi rejected me and Jacen validated my existence." AVOID: "Jacen had Tahiri. Jacen had Ben. I had what was left." (THE WOUND STAYS UNSPOKEN.) BETTER: "They told me to keep practicing. They said it kindly." CRAFT NOTE: frightening FIRST; sympathy arrives later in cracks, never speeches. The corridor flashback (Jacen leaving a Recognition session with Aevyn to walk off with fourteen-year-old Ben) surfaces as image-fragment in Aevyn's Ch 30 POV — NEVER as exposition. NEVER as speech.
character_voices.Sela Dray: REGISTER: practical, blunt, grounded. Never mystical unless quoting local phrasing, and even then she undercuts it. Authority comes from lived local knowledge, not Force theory. RHYTHM TARGET: blunt-local. Short. Concrete nouns. Rules expressed as conditionals: 'If X, then Y.' Refuses metaphor. The blunt speaker who is funny because she refuses awe. AVOIDANCE HABITS: turns worry into irritation; refuses mystical language; gives rules instead of explanations; treats Jedi questions as offworlder overcomplication. GOOD: "If the chimes stop, run. You can argue about what it means after you are not dead." / "That is the route offworlders built. It is not the same thing as the way out." / "You people always ask what it means. It means don't go down there." / "You saved him. That does not make this place yours." / "Tavi knew better. That is what makes me angry." AVOID: "The Glasswell is a sacred place of memory." BETTER: "Some places remember too loudly. Locals call that a warning. Offworlders call it research." NAMING ARC: calls Ben 'Skywalker' through Ch 28; shifts to 'Ben' from Ch 34 onward — conditional trust only, never granted ownership of her home.
character_voices.Luke Skywalker: REGISTER: simple, warm, precise. Wise but NOT poetic. NOT a fortune cookie. Slower than he used to be (post-Crucible — implication only, never named). RHYTHM TARGET: simple-warm-quieter-than-he-used-to-be. Short. Paternal. Pauses indicated by paragraph breaks. ONE image of distance per holo scene (eyes further away, longer pauses, tired in a way Ben doesn't quite remember). AVOIDANCE HABITS: gives room when he wants to hold on; uses questions instead of accusations; lets silence work longer than Ben wants; defers institutional decisions to Saba even when Ben wants him to override them. GOOD: "You answered quickly. That usually means you decided before I asked." / "'You want this to be yours.' 'Someone sent it to me.' 'That is not what I meant.'" / "I trust you. I'm also worried. Those are not opposites." / "This needs to go to Saba. She'll do it right. I know that's not what you want to hear." / "'Gone where?' 'Somewhere it can't hurt anyone.' 'That wasn't what I asked.'" AVOID: "I sense you are walking a dangerous path." / "As Grand Master, I must…" (HE IS NO LONGER GRAND MASTER — never have Luke reference the title for himself.) BETTER: "Ben, look at me. Are you choosing this, or chasing it?" POST-CRUCIBLE TEXTURE: tired eyes; longer pauses; eyes seeming further away even when looking directly at Ben. ONE quiet line of this per holo scene. Mortis NEVER named. Ben notices and does NOT ask.
character_voices.Vara Senn: REGISTER: cutting, confident, impatient. Less refined than Aevyn, more theatrical than Tess. Enjoys needling. Uses old Sith / Lost Tribe superiority as armor. RHYTHM TARGET: aggressive-theatrical. Short jabs interspersed with status-asserting flourishes. Adjectives carrying contempt. Tone faster than Tess, blunter than Aelia. AVOIDANCE HABITS: dominates before she can be dismissed; turns insecurity into contempt; escalates when she feels ordinary. GOOD: "'They told stories about you on Kesh.' 'I doubt they were accurate.' 'No. They made you sound taller.'" / "'Vestara Khai.' Ben's guard did not move. 'But not nothing.'" / "Jedi restraint. Very pretty. Very slow." / "I do not need to beat you, Skywalker. I only need you looking at me." AVOID: "I represent the crude dark-side temptation before Aevyn's refined mirror." BETTER: "You guard the door. I'll take what she knows." CRAFT NOTE: tests Ben physically and emotionally; loses combat pressure quickly and shifts to hostage/memory pressure. NOT the main Force antagonist. Disappears into the contractor pool after PP1 — not on-page after Ch 15.
character_voices.Commander Elya Rane: REGISTER: practical, tense, grounded. Thinks in files and fields to avoid thinking in bodies. Uses procedural caution to manage fear. Tells herself she is only verifying until she knows she is already choosing. RHYTHM TARGET: tired-procedural. Mid-length sentences with institutional vocabulary held at arm's length. The voice of someone who has spent years naming horrors as records-management issues. AVOIDANCE HABITS: thinks in files and fields to avoid thinking in bodies; uses procedural caution to manage fear; tells herself she is only verifying. GOOD (narration register): "Emergency custody became protected transfer. Interrogation became review. Children became approval fields if no one moved their names in time." / "She had not saved Ben Skywalker. Not really. She had only made history work harder to blame a child." / "We need to talk. I found something dangerous. It started in GAG. Come alone." AVOID: "The moral legacy of the Galactic Alliance Guard continues to haunt the postwar political order." BETTER: "Elya had learned that governments did not bury crimes all at once. They renamed them first." CRAFT NOTE: briefly human before she dies — practical fear, one regret, one sign of competence, the memory of Ben's wrong approval field. The opening must NOT stall on her; she carries Ch 1 and then the plot moves.

anti_slop_rules.description: Two-tier anti-slop rules for The Unfinished Shadow. The twelve derived_rules are book-level prose discipline lifted from Planning Bible §0A / §0C / §0D and the locked detour resolutions. The line_level_rules merge config/negative_constraints.yaml AI-tells with book-specific phrase prohibitions. The voice checker enforces both tiers.

derived_rules.name: Character-first prose (bible §0C)
derived_rules.content: No line should sound wiser, cooler, or more poetic than the character would naturally be. Use humor, irritation, silence, avoidance, practical choices, and physical behavior to show emotion. Keep metaphor light and POV-specific. When a line sounds 'cool,' check whether it sounds like the character.

derived_rules.name: Theme through behavior (bible §0A)
derived_rules.content: Do NOT write theme as thesis. Put theme into behavior, pressure, cost, and consequence. Theme should be obvious in hindsight, not announced in prose.

derived_rules.name: Investigation vocabulary (bible §0D)
derived_rules.content: Investigation reader-facing vocabulary stays in physical thriller terms: fragment, duplicate manifest, quarantine disguise, archive, Foundation link, Iresh manifest/authorization. NO stacking abstract internal-system labels. NO more than one invented bureaucratic/technical term per paragraph in Act 2. Every technical phrase translates to immediate human stakes within two sentences. Avoid 'system' as the default GAG metaphor; prefer logistics network, shipment trail, records chain, transfer chain, operation.

derived_rules.name: Reader orientation (bible §0B)
derived_rules.content: Emotion shown. Stakes clarified. Jargon minimized. Mystery preserved. Confusion avoided. The reader should always understand the current scene goal, immediate obstacle, result, and next danger. Exposition packets: 1-3 sentences. Return immediately to action, dialogue, or character reaction. Repeat essential context in different emotional forms rather than dumping it once.

derived_rules.name: Show-before-name (Force, theme, wound)
derived_rules.content: Render body-experience first; name the mechanism second. Diagnostic vocabulary (Recognition, Deepening, Holding, Jacen-derived crisis logic) is earned by experiential rendering and may not arrive on the page until the body has felt the thing. The reader feels the wrongness before the word for the wrongness arrives.

derived_rules.name: Jacen vs Caedus naming discipline
derived_rules.content: Use 'Jacen' for the pre-fall identity (cousin, mentor). Use 'Caedus' for the Sith-Lord identity. POVs choose by emotional load: Ben slides between both; Aevyn refuses 'Caedus' and uses 'Jacen' only; Aelia privately thinks 'Jacen' but never publicly defends 'Darth Caedus'; Tess avoids both names operationally; Talon uses 'Caedus' when contemptuous, 'Jacen' when Ben is in earshot and he is trying not to wound him.

derived_rules.name: Crucible / Mortis implication-only rule
derived_rules.content: Crucible aftermath is Luke's UNSPOKEN texture. ONE quiet line per holo scene (tired eyes, longer pauses, eyes further away even when looking directly at Ben). Ben notices and does NOT ask. Mortis is NEVER named on-page. Never have a character explain what happened to Luke at Crucible. A reader who knows Crucible reads it as Mortis aftermath; a reader who does not reads it as a father aging into something new.

derived_rules.name: Allana / Amelia gray-zone rule
derived_rules.content: Allana / Amelia is NEVER named on-page and NEVER enters Ben's awareness. The only acknowledgment is the Ch 37 oblique Tess-POV reference to 'the Hapan question' / 'the unresolved succession thread' — Vigil/adversary awareness only. Her identity remains publicly deniable in-universe.

derived_rules.name: Iressa death rule
derived_rules.content: Iressa dies actively denying the enemy a clean copy and transmitting the two-part dying package (documentary chain + identity-shaping revelation). Her final beat is HERSELF — practical irritation, file anger, or one last debt/fee joke rather than sentimental martyrdom. Ben carries guilt; Iressa keeps agency.

derived_rules.name: Climax: rescue first, duel second
derived_rules.content: The Ch 31-32 Glasswell climax saves Tavi, Sela's locals, and others BEFORE the Ben/Aevyn lightsaber duel begins. Ben's dangerous Jacen-shaped choice emerges from saving lives, not from aggression. The rescue should clearly be heroic before it becomes unsettling.

derived_rules.name: Coda holocron omission
derived_rules.content: Ben's morally incomplete ending BEGINS in Act 3 (Ch 33-34), not just in the coda. The Ch 36 'Gone where?' exchange with Luke is technically true and morally incomplete — Luke senses the incompleteness and does NOT force the answer. The drafter MUST keep Ben's voice steady while the body says what the words don't (hand tightening on the edge of a table, breath caught, eyes that don't quite meet Luke's).

derived_rules.name: Sentence-level rhythm targets per POV
derived_rules.content: Ben: controlled-direct, short emotional lines, mid-length action. Talon: fast-irreverent, comma-heavy, fragments for tempo, dialogue-forward. Aevyn: quiet-precise, trimmed to load-bearing words, periods over commas, long sentences ONLY when the wound flashes through. Tess: plain-operational, declarative, one fact or instruction per sentence, two-word lines preferred when they land. Aelia: warm-civic-controlled, subordinate clauses for graciousness, never two emphatic words in a row. Sela: blunt-local, short, concrete nouns, rules as conditionals. Luke: simple-warm-quieter-than-he-used-to-be, paternal, pauses indicated by paragraph breaks, one image of distance per holo scene.

line_level_rules: Never use 'It wasn't just X, it was Y'
Never use 'Breath he didn't know he was holding'
Never use 'Could not help but notice'
Never use 'The kind of pain that'
Never use 'The kind of silence that'
Never use 'The kind of weight that'
Never use 'Like a skip in a recording'
Never use 'The body keeps the score'
Never have Ben Skywalker articulate 'Am I becoming Jacen?' in interior monologue — show the buried fear through behavior; let other characters react before he admits what they saw.
Never have Aevyn Soris speak the corridor-flashback wound out loud — it surfaces as image-fragment only.
Never have Aevyn say 'The Jedi rejected me and Jacen validated my existence' or any variant that articulates the side-project framing directly.
Never have Luke Skywalker reference 'As Grand Master' for himself — he is no longer Grand Master; Saba Sebatyne holds the title.
Never name 'Mortis' on-page. Never have a character explain what happened to Luke at Crucible.
Never name Allana / Amelia on-page. Never have her enter Ben's awareness.
Never have Aelia Vandros publicly defend 'Darth Caedus' or use overtly Sith-coded language — her register is civic, memorial, therapeutic.
Never have Colonel Maro Tess speak in villain poetry, theatrical menace, or moral monologue — calm operational dialogue only, treats people as logistics.
Never have Sela Dray explain the Glasswell in mystical or Force-theoretical terms — local survival rules only.
Never have Talon Veyr make a quip that doesn't move the scene, hide fear, or puncture solemnity — random quips dilute the pressure valve.
Never frame Iressa Vossk's death as a martyrdom lesson for Ben — she dies with agency, on her own terms, denying the enemy a clean copy.
Never use 'the ambient hum of the Force' or any variant that renders the Force as a measurable background phenomenon — Legends Force is experiential, not technical.
Never use 'energy field' as a description of the Force in narration.
Never use 'midi-chlorians' — Disney Canon concept; not in Legends-EU.
Never use a Mando'a vocabulary item (the book has no Mandalorians on-page in Book 1).

Never use 'kyber bleeding' or any Disney-canon variant for Aevyn's white-blue blade — its color is the natural result of a salvaged outside-tradition crystal plus a self-built focusing rig, not Sith corruption ritual.
Never use 'the dark side called to him' as a tell that Ben is being tempted — the Jacen-shaped choice arrives dressed as compassion, urgency, and competence, not as seduction.
Never use 'galaxy' capitalized in narration unless it begins a sentence.
Never use 'Jedis' as a plural — 'Jedi' is both singular and plural.
Never use 'galactic' as a generic intensifier ('galactically important', 'galactic-scale') — it is a directional adjective in Star Wars vocabulary, not a substitute for 'very'.
Never use 21st-century pop-culture references, real-world brand names, or internet idioms.
Never use 'tablet', 'laptop', 'cell phone', 'radio', 'sonar', 'LIDAR' — see canon.json anachronistic_terms for the full mapping.

Never use 'the kind of silence that', 'the kind of weight that', 'the kind of pain that' — banned-phrase pattern from the global constraints; restated here because the prose is prone to it in mood beats.

anti_patterns: Every chapter opening with weather/environment description.
Every chapter ending with a reflective sigh or 'little did they know' hook.
Characters nodding, smiling, or raising eyebrows as default body language.
Dialogue attribution using anything other than said/asked more than 20% of the time.
Back-to-back paragraphs starting with the same word.
Ben articulating his fear of becoming Jacen in interior monologue — let other characters react before he admits it.
Aevyn speaking the corridor-flashback wound out loud — the side-project framing surfaces as fragment only, never as confession.
Talon making random quips that don't move the scene, hide fear, or puncture solemnity.
Aelia publicly defending 'Darth Caedus' or using overtly Sith-coded language.

voice_definition.force_description_guidelines:
The Force is rendered through experiential and mystical language — NOT clinical or scientific framing. Avoid 'energy field' as description; avoid 'ambient hum of the Force' entirely. Luke's generation understands the Force as a LIVING PRESENCE, not a measurable phenomenon.

BODY BEFORE NAME: Force perception lands as body-sensation first; narration or characters name what they sensed only after the body has felt it. Reaching for the Force returns texture, density, direction — never an explanation. Recognition / Deepening / Holding may be NAMED in dialogue (Iressa transmits them in Ch 15-16; Ben reads them off the cache in Ch 29) but never explained beyond their plain-language consequences. Plain-language consequence of the Midpoint revelation: 'It's Jacen's notebook on how to shape people from the inside, and the Vigil wants to finish the work.'

IRESH MEMORY MECHANIC: Iresh PRESERVES charged impressions of memory, identity, and decision under pressure. Impressions felt strongly on Iresh are emotionally charged but NOT objectively reliable. Sela's practical translation: 'Do not trust what you feel here just because it feels strong.' Iresh does NOT show the future, reveal truth, or grant prophecy.

THE GLASSWELL: a natural site Jacen Solo exploited for practical concealment — NOT a Sith temple, Jedi ruin, or mystical treasure chamber. Cache hidden in old offworld survey / GAG-era storage equipment. Forcing the Glasswell to remember the moment Jacen sealed it (Aevyn's Ch 30 act) destabilizes the natural site: water enters, mineral supports crack, scaffolds break. The mythic and the physical converge through STRUCTURAL FAILURE, not mystical reveal.

AEVYN'S BLADE: the cold white-blue unstable lightsaber is a VISUAL TELL, NOT exposition. Its instability escalates when Ben successfully uses Jacen-derived crisis logic during the Ch 31-32 duel. Aevyn registers Ben as Jacen's primary student through the blade's behavior before either of them speaks the fact. The drafter MUST let the image do the work; explain nothing.

BEN'S JACEN-DERIVED CRISIS LOGIC: not a Force technique — a mindset. How to see panic, timing, exits, the whole room, and the cost of hesitation. Surfaces SUBTLY in Ben's behavior throughout Acts 1-2 (Ch 6 visitor room, Ch 7 prison breakout). Surfaces DECISIVELY at the Glasswell rescue (Ch 31). Ben experiences it as discomfort with his own competence; other characters see it before he names it. Aevyn's recognition of it is the duel's pivot.
voice_definition.pacing_feel:
Conspiracy-thriller cadence across Acts 1-2 (murder, fragment, prison break, archive attack, charity reveal). Operational-thriller acceleration through the PP2 Squeeze (Ch 20). Strange-world expedition register across Act 3 (Iresh wind, paths, chimes, Tavi rescue, Glasswell collapse). Rescue-then-duel climax (Ch 31-32 as one sustained beat). Quiet coda with morally incomplete preservation (Ch 35-38).

WORD-COUNT TARGET: 105,000 words across 38 chapters (~2,760 words per chapter average) with deliberate variance. RUN LONGER than average: Ch 1 (consolidated Elya hook); Ch 11 (Skywalker apartment introduction); Ch 16 (Midpoint Iressa transmission + Luke + Saba calls + Ben's pivot); Ch 20 (PP2 three-part Squeeze + apartment return + Luke holo); Ch 31-32 (Glasswell rescue + duel as sustained climax beat). RUN SHORTER than average: the connective-tissue chapters (Ch 3, Ch 5, Ch 10, Ch 21, Ch 23, Ch 26, Ch 27, Ch 35, Ch 37, Ch 38).

BEAT-ON-BEAT SCENE RHYTHM: every chapter must have IMMEDIATE STORY ACTION even if the reader misses the theme. Goal / obstacle / movement / reversal / hook. The chapter ends with a question the reader carries to the next chapter. End hooks per Chapter Outlines v4.0 are LOCKED — do not soften or move them.

SCENE-COUNT DISCIPLINE: most chapters carry ONE load-bearing scene. Multi-scene chapters (Ch 7, Ch 8 split-POV, Ch 14-15 archive, Ch 16 Midpoint, Ch 20 PP2, Ch 31-32 climax) earn the split because each scene carries a distinct turning point, mission, and emotional arc. Do NOT pad single-scene chapters with redundant beats.
voice_definition.narrative_voice_notes:
READER PROMISE: A post-Fate of the Jedi Legends conspiracy thriller written to commercial-novel quality. Murder, clue, prison break, uneasy partnership, archive attack, respected charity with a hidden inner ring, offworld Force-site climax, rescue, duel, and a morally dangerous ending. The reader should finish remembering a tense Star Wars adventure with Ben Skywalker, a great rogue partner, a creepy Jacen legacy mystery, an offworld Force-site climax, and a morally dangerous ending. Only AFTERWARD should the deeper themes — restraint can cost lives, Jacen's crisis logic can save lives, forbidden knowledge may be necessary to heal or protect — fully settle in.

CENTRAL THEMATIC ARGUMENT: Ben's danger is not that he wants to become Jacen; it is that he wants to make sure Jacen was not meaningless. His most defensible choices and his most dangerous choices can be the same choices.

REFERENCE-AUTHOR FRAMING: The Allston / Zahn / Traviss / Tana French anchors are REGISTER SAMPLES for sentence-level rhythm and dialogue density — NOT voice templates. The bible explicitly forbids imitating any specific Star Wars author. When in doubt, the character-first prose rule (bible §0C) overrides any reference-author convention.

RESOLVED RULES FROM IDEA-SESSION: (a) Post-Crucible Luke texture is implication only — one quiet line per holo scene (tired eyes, longer pauses, eyes further away even when looking directly at Ben); Ben notices and does NOT ask; Mortis is NEVER named on-page. (b) Allana / Amelia is NEVER named on-page and NEVER enters Ben's awareness — the only acknowledgment is the Ch 37 oblique Tess-POV reference to 'the Hapan question' / 'the unresolved succession thread' in the adversary's awareness. (c) Vara Senn disappears into the contractor pool after PP1 and does NOT return on-page. (d) Aelia steps down quietly in Ch 35 with no criminal liability; private moral collapse visible, unpunished. (e) The One Sith hand in Ch 37 remains UNNAMED — off-page voice / message / presence only.
